title: Show HN: A working Nintendo in ~1GB of Qwen weights
abstract:
nesformer An NES CPU compiled into the weights of a stock Qwen3.5 model. The NES's 6502 CPU (the core of its 2A03 chip), its 2 KB of work RAM, and a cartridge's program
ROM run inside a standard Qwen3_5ForCausalLM checkpoint. Nobody trained these weights; a
compiler computed every one. When you play a game, the model predicts the CPU's execution log
one token at a time. A small host program plays the rest of the console around it: it draws the
picture, reads the controller, and fires the vblank interrupt. nesformer builds on Qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal , which
compiled a CHIP-8 and then a RISC-V CPU into Qwen3.5-4B. It reuses Qwenputer's compiler and its
central trick: the model's Gated DeltaNet state is the machine's memory. Super Mario Bros. (World 1-1) Full Game by Doug Fraker (title screen and first level) Every CPU token in these runs came from the model. For the bundled test games, every frame also
matches a conventional 6502 emulator's output exactly (see How it was checked ). Quick start 1. Folder layout Unzip nesformer.zip and nesformer-weights.zip into the same folder. The weights go next to the nesformer/ package, not inside it: nesformer/ <- run commands from here
├── nesformer/ <- the Python package
├── chipformer/ <- Qwenputer's compiler
├── roms/ <- test ROMs (put your own here too)
├── examples/ <- sample GIFs and frame sheets
├── tests/
├── LICENSE
├── LICENSE.chipformer
├── README.md
├── pyproject.toml
└── weights/ <- from nesformer-weights.zip ├── config.json ├── generation_config.json ├── model.safetensors ├── nesformer.json └── SHA256SUMS The CLI looks for weights/ beside the nesformer/ package. To keep the weights elsewhere,
pass --weights /path/to/weights to run , check or trace , or give the path to info . To confirm the weights unzipped correctly, run shasum -a 256 -c weights/SHA256SUMS from the
top folder. 2. Install You need Python 3.11 or newer. python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate pip install numpy scipy numba pillow 3. Play a game python -m nesformer run roms/thwaite.nes --frames 600 --show \ --buttons " start@90-95+200-205,a@230-233+250-253+270-273+290-293+310-313+330-333+350-353+370-373+390-393+410-413+430-433+450-453+470-473+490-493+510-513+530-533+550-553+570-573+590-593 " --show draws each frame in your terminal as the model generates it. When the run ends, the CLI
saves an animated GIF named after the ROM (here thwaite.gif ) in the current folder. Expect it to be slow. The first run spends about 20 seconds compiling the engine with numba.
After that, a frame takes 1–6 seconds, so 600 frames (10 seconds of NES time) take around
25 minutes. Playing your own ROMs Point run at any .nes file that uses the NROM board (iNES mapper 0), such as Super Mario
Bros., Donkey Kong or Excitebike. You supply the ROM; nesformer only ships the three freely
licensed test ROMs in roms/ . python -m nesformer run roms/smb.nes --frames 600 --show \ --buttons " start@60-65,right@200-600,a@250-265+300-315+360-375+420-435+480-495+540-555 " That script starts the game, then walks Mario right and jumps about once a second. The CLI loads
the ROM into the model's state at startup, so the same weights run any NROM game without a
rebuild. Games on other boards stop with a message: see Limitations . Controller scripts --buttons takes a comma-separated list of entries. Each entry names one or more buttons joined
by + , then @ , then one or more frame ranges joined by + : start@60-65 press Start during frames 60 to 65
right@200-600 hold Right from frame 200 to frame 600
a@250-265+300-315 press A twice
right+b@200-600 hold Right and B together (run, in Super Mario Bros.) The buttons are a , b , select , start , up , down , left and right . Frames count from
power-on at 60 per second, so frame 600 is 10 seconds in. Games ignore input on screens where
you can't move, so holding a button a little early does no harm. In Super Mario Bros., a longer
A press makes a higher jump. Commands Command What it does python -m nesformer run ROM Play a ROM on the weights and save a GIF python -m nesformer check ROM Run the weights and the reference CPU side by side; stop at the first difference python -m nesformer trace ROM Print the model's token stream (default 40 tokens) python -m nesformer build Compile the circuit and write weights/ (about 10 seconds) python -m nesformer info Describe the checkpoint Options for run : Option Default Meaning --frames N 120 Stop after N frames --buttons SCRIPT none Controller input (see above) --show off Draw frames in the terminal (needs 24-bit color, e.g. iTerm2 or Windows Terminal) --gif PATH ROM name Where to save the animated GIF --png DIR off Save each kept frame as a PNG in DIR. With --png alone, no GIF is saved. Add --gif to get both. --every N 1 Keep every N-th frame --scale N 2 Enlarge saved frames N times --engine fast fast (numba), numpy , or hf (stock transformers; needs torch, ~10 tokens/s) --no-skip off Run every iteration of idle wait loops (slower; identical frames) --max-tokens N none Stop after N tokens --trace FILE none Save the token ids run , check and trace all accept --weights , --engine , --buttons and --no-skip . check --tokens N sets how far to compare (default 50,000). trace --tokens N sets how many
tokens to print (default 40). build --out DIR writes the checkpoint somewhere other than weights/ . How it works What's in the weights, and what isn't In the model (weights + DeltaNet state) In the host ( nesformer/host.py ) The 6502 core: all 151 official opcodes, every addressing mode, flags, stack, BRK and NMI entry The PPU: a scanline renderer and the palette 2 KB of work RAM Controllers; APU registers (written, otherwise ignored) 32 KB of PRG-ROM, stored twice: one copy for instruction fetch, one for data reads NMI timing at vblank, injected as an NMI token OAM DMA reads (the 256 bytes appear as DM tokens) Answers to I/O reads, injected as IN tokens This split follows Qwenputer's CHIP-8 build, whose host injects timer ticks and draws the
display from the trace. The host never sees the CPU's registers or RAM except through the trace. The memory trick works like this. Each DeltaNet head keeps a 128 × 128 state matrix that the
delta rule updates at every token. With the gate held open and a one-hot key, an update
overwrites exactly one row of that matrix, and a one-hot query reads it back. So every row is a
memory cell, and the cartridge, RAM and registers all live in rows. The checkpoint weights/ is an ordinary Hugging Face folder. It loads with Qwen3_5ForCausalLM.from_pretrained and needs no custom code. Architecture Qwen3_5ForCausalLM , with Qwen3.5-4B's DeltaNet head shapes (16 key heads, 32 value heads, dim 128) and MLP width (9,216) Layers 7 Gated DeltaNet layers (the circuit), plus 1 all-zero attention layer that Hugging Face's cache needs Hidden size 768 Vocabulary 263,808 tokens Parameters 466.6M in bf16 (933 MB), of which 9.3M are nonzero , so the weights zip to 3.3 MB nesformer.json records which layer and head holds each part of the machine. A run writes the
cartridge, registers and RAM into those DeltaNet states, then decodes greedily. Layer plan Layer Attention (state) MLP 1 PC anchor; instruction counters; A, X, Y, SP; flags N V Z C I D; pointer latches; NMI flag counter thermometers; SP ± 1; LO + Y 2 — PC = anchor + bytes executed since; PC + 1, PC + 2 3 PRG fetch: opcode and two operand bytes at the PC opcode decode; operand bits; indexed sums; branch test and target 4 — effective address, by addressing mode and record stage; the byte a push stores 5 RAM and PRG data reads at the effective address operand; ADC/SBC adder, compares, BIT; address decode 6 — result byte, carry, overflow, flags, jump targets 7 — the next token The trace Each instruction becomes a record, and the record's last token commits it.

title: Why Did Meta Suspend a US Senate Candidate's Instagram in the Middle of a Rally?
abstract:
Most Recent Post Meta suspended a Latino outreach Instagram account for Florida Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon without explanation just days before the midterms, stoking even more allegations that the massive social media company is meddling in elections. “Hey @Meta 👋We are currently hosting a get-out-the-vote rally in Osceola County, home to a large Puerto Rican community, and our #LatinosConAngie @instagram page was suddenly taken down while we were actively posting content from the event,” Nixon wrote Tuesday evening on X. “This page is a critical communication tool for reaching Latino voters and mobilizing our community. With just seven days until Election Day, every minute matters. “We are calling on Meta to immediately restore the page and provide an explanation for its removal,” she continued. “Voters deserve access to critical election information, especially in these final days.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by We the American People ❌👑 (@50501movement) Nixon reported that the account was back up an hour later. This comes after Meta’s own employees accused the massive social media company of suppressing the campaign of leftist Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, while outside sources found it was “ actively boosting ” right-wing candidate Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign with its algorithm. Meta also shut down the No Kings Instagram account the weekend of the group’s midterm protests, and gave the same treatment to Serbian accounts critical of right-wing President Aleksandar Vučić earlier this year. Meta has donated $5 million to President Trump’s White House ballroom fund and $1 million to his inauguration fund. Editor’s Pick: Can This Florida Dem Pull Off One More Big Surprise? Most Recent Post Tennessee state Senator Brent Taylor’s adolescence must have run a bit longer than the rest of humanity’s. Taylor is the Republican nominee for the Volunteer State’s 9th congressional district and has been endorsed by Donald Trump. He is simultaneously running for reelection in the Tennessee state Senate, hoping to continue to represent district 31, which covers parts of Memphis and the southwestern portion of the state. (If he wins both races, he will have to resign from one of the seats, prompting a special election to replace him.) He has been in politics since 1995, when he was 27 years old, and has framed himself as a Christian family man and a committed husband. But Taylor’s dual campaign—and his regional reputation—was torn to bits Tuesday when he confessed to sending unsolicited nudes and then proceeded to brush off the wanton behavior as a simple mistake of his youth. “As I near 60 years old, the expiration date has come and gone on any of my youthful indiscretions,” Taylor told the Nashville Scene when asked about the unsolicited nudes allegation. “Whatever story you think you’ve got, my wife is well aware of, and we’ve worked through it a long time ago.” “My God and my wife have forgiven me, and I would consider everyone else doing the same,” Taylor added. title: Tell HN: Scribd Breached
abstract:

Hello, We are writing to let you know that Scribd, Inc. recently experienced a security incident that may have affected your data. We detected that an unauthorized third party may have gained access to certain user data in one of our systems. After investigating this activity, we found that the third party may have accessed your email address and the following of your information: last 4 digits of your credit card and country, credit card issuer, credit card expiry date, payment history (not including credit card details). We have no evidence that this data has been misused, but we are notifying you out of an abundance of caution so that you can take steps to protect your information. title: The oldest ice disappears and the Stone Age emerges from it
abstract:
The oldest ice is disappearing: The Stone Age is emerging from the melting ice 'We have been at the edge of the ice. We have seen it happening. And we are witnesses to a rapidly changing archaeological landscape,' write the glacial archaeologists. Finds from the Viking Age are becoming scarce, while 6,000-year-old arrowheads are now emerging from the melting ice. A 5,000-year-old arrowhead made of slate, found together with parts of its shaft right at the edge of the ice. Domesticated reindeer can be seen on the ice patch in the background. (Photo: Åsa Rommetveit Celius / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice) Ida Irene Bergstrøm Ida Irene Bergstrøm Journalist Published 26 September 2026 - 00:01 For exactly 20 years, archaeologists working with Secrets of the Ice have been recovering and preserving artefacts emerging from the ice in the mountains of Innlandet, eastern Norway. Until now, most of the objects have been up to 2,000 years old. Many date from the Viking Age. But the ancient ice is now beginning to melt. And within this oldest ice lie the oldest finds: large quantities of arrow shafts and arrowheads from the Bronze Age and the Stone Age. A bone arrowhead found together with parts of its shaft right beside the ice. Approximately 5,000 years old. (Photo: Frys Film / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice) An arrowhead made from a freshwater mussel shell, dating from the Bronze Age, approximately 3,600 years old. The arrowhead is fragile and has begun to split apart. (Photo: Frys film / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice) Here comes the Stone Age Annonse One of the oldest finds from this year's first field expedition is an arrow with an arrowhead and shaft made of slate. By comparing it with previously discovered arrows, archaeologists estimate that it is between 5,000 and 6,000 years old. The fact that arrows are emerging from the melting ice is not surprising. Over the 20 years they have been working here, the archaeologists have found extensive evidence of reindeer and reindeer hunting . They have also found clothing, shoes , dead packhorses, and a pair of skis . The preservation conditions in the ice have meant that organic material, such as wood, leather, and textiles, have also survived. “This year, we found 48 prehistoric arrows. That's a lot,” Espen Finstad, who leads Secrets of the Ice, tells Science Norway. He explains that, with these latest discoveries, more than 100 arrowheads and arrow shafts have now been recovered from a single ice patch over the years. The oldest arrowheads are made from slate, freshwater mussel shells, and bone. More recent arrowheads are made from iron and are 'only' between 1,000 and 1,500 years old. Archaeologist Åsa Rommetveit Celius from Innlandet County Municipality documents the discovery of a 1,000-year-old arrow shaft. (Photo: May-Tove Smiseth / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice) Archaeologist Kjetil Loftsgarden from the Museum of Cultural History in Oslo holds a complete 1,800-year-old arrow with a bone arrowhead and a wooden shaft. (Photo: Espen Finstad / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice) A brutal backdrop But this year’s fieldwork carries an added sense of gravity. Finstad explains that the work of recovering archaeological artefacts from the ice has always carried a certain duality. “It’s fun going around looking for things. It’s exciting, and finding something is just really cool," he says. Yet behind the excitement lies the reality of climate change. Finstad points to the recent landslide in Nepal and the glacier collapse in Jotunheimen. “We have always acknowledged this contradiction and the reality behind our work. But this is the first time it has truly affected us on an emotional level,” Finstad says, adding: “This year, there was a much deeper sense of seriousness and sadness. Only patches of ice remain where we once had large ice patches. It's brutal. And this year, that reality struck us more forcefully than ever before." Annonse Participants in the field from the Glacier Archaeology Programme in Innlandet, Secrets of the Ice. (Photo: Frys Film / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice) The glacial archaeologists’ tent camp in Jotunheimen at sunrise. Fresh snow on the ground. (Photo: Espen Finstad / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice) Finstad and his colleagues estimate that most of the ice patches containing archaeological artefacts will have disappeared within the next 20 years. “There has been ice here for 6,000–7,000 years. Nature has been warning us and sending signals for many years. But now it's giving up. Now it is simply going to melt,” says the glacial archaeologist. 'For thousands of years, ancient ice has safely preserved unique objects from the past. Now that ice is disappearing,' the archaeologists write in a press release about the finds. 'We have been at the edge of the ice. We have seen it happening. And we are witnesses to a rapidly changing archaeological landscape.' Se dette innlegget på Instagram Et innlegg delt av forskning.no (@forskning.no) The lower section of one of the ice patches at Hanklefonne. It was once large. Now only a small, steep section remains. 'The ice is disappearing much faster than we expected. The landscape has changed dramatically, and large areas that were recently covered by ice are now ice-free,' the glacial archaeologists write in a press release. (Photo: Espen Finstad / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice) More fieldwork ahead Finstad and his colleagues are planning more fieldwork in the coming weeks, weather permitting. So far, they have secured finds in the Kvittingskjølen mountain area of Jotunheimen, specifically at Langfonne, Storefonne, and Hanklefonne. Several of the finds are already on display at the Norwegian Mountain Centre in Lom, just a few days after they were discovered. ——— Translated by Alette Bjordal Gjellesvik Read the Norwegian version of this article on forskning.no Related content A 1,300-year-old arrow and horse dung have emerged from a melting Norwegian glacier Melting ice near Norway's highest mountain reveals horse bridle that could stem from the Viking Age Subscribe to our newsletter The latest news from Science Norway, sent twice a week and completely free. title: Prospero: A new coding harness for a more civilized age
abstract:
Prospero: a new coding harness for a more civilized age October 31, 2026 nullprogram.com/blog/2026/10/31/ I’ve been fascinated with local LLMs for a couple of years now.
The better open weight models, including some that inference on regular,
higher-end consumer hardware at tolerable speeds, are now reliable enough
to handle simpler programming tasks. This requires a coding harness, but
so far this year I’ve been disappointed by all the harness offerings. For
inexplicable reasons most are built with web stacks, and consume enormous
amounts of memory. At its core a coding harness is essentially curl glued
to popen() . This should not require gigabytes of RAM. So I built my own: Prospero . It’s written in my C++ style with a snappy Dear
ImGui docking interface . It uses around two orders of magnitude
fewer resources than other harnesses without sacrificing features. Dark mode aficionados are covered, too: Note that Prospero comes with no model providers built-in. You’re expected
to supply that yourself, such as with llama.cpp , a workplace on-prem
model, OpenRouter, Anthropic API, OpenAI API, etc. (You can’t use your
Claude subscription.) For those unfamiliar with coding harnesses: In a chat interface you and
the AI take turns writing messages to each other. A coding harness extends
this concept, allowing an AI to “talk” to tools offered by the harness.
Tools “reply” with their outputs. A tool might read or write a file, or
run a shell command. An AI will go from tool call to tool call on its own,
looping on the results. Such an AI is called an agent . Occasionally the
AI will send you a message to inform you of progress or to ask a question,
and the chat interface is still there. Some harnesses, including Prospero, allow agents to spawn subagents to
do their bidding, to work in parallel or keep their context clean. That
is, to not fill their working memory with subtasks. Agents can message one
another and coordinate on tasks. Given SSH access to another machine, or
over plain WSL, Prospero can deploy a headless copy of itself to other
hosts so that agents can operate on those systems. The Professional
Edition embeds engines for combinations of x86/x86-64 and ARM64 on
macOS, Windows, and Linux. The Windows x86 engine even works on Windows
XP, and can play solitaire and minesweeper if you ask. The last is because Prospero is one of the few harnesses with desktop
control capabilities. If your model supports vision — any any model worth
using does — then it can “see” your desktop and interact with it. It can
click, type, and drag to test and debug GUI applications live without a
specialized, per-app MCP assist . This headless engine is why no TUI is necessary. The harness engine runs
on the headless system, and the UI runs on your desktop or laptop. With a
little extra setup, the harness to run fully independently of the GUI, so
that it will continue without the GUI system attached — re-attachable
later. Because Prospero is so lean, it may be the only harness that can drive a fuzz campaign , particularly on a headless system, without the
Linux OOM killer targeting the memory-gobbling harness rather than the
out-of-control fuzz target that triggered it. So many times I’ve checked
back in on a fuzz campaign hours later, to find nothing was accomplished
because the harness process is gone. (Why have an agent run a fuzz campaign? Because it can fix discovered bugs
on the fly and keep the campaign going! It’s a no brainer.) Configuration The configuration lives at ~/.config/prospero/prospero.ini . Easy to
edit. No JSON, thank goodness. Check it into source control, copy-paste
it. All the usual benefits. Alternatively, the Settings page can reach
every setting from the GUI, so you don’t have to edit the INI by hand. INI
files can also include each other, not just naming file system paths but
URLs: include = https://example.com/prospero.ini The idea is to allow a live shared or managed configuration. Includes by
URL are restricted in what they can set, with a hard rule against anything
which might appear in shell command. Some trust is still required, as a
configuration can extract an environment variable by using it as an API
key and supplying an endpoint it controls. Prospero fetches a model list and other parameters like context size from
the endpoint, but you might want to tweak it. A typical configuration may
look like: model = falstaff/Qwen3.8-27B [endpoint falstaff] url = http://falstaff.local/ key = env:FALSTAFF_API_KEY [model Qwen3.8-27B] edit_format = replace template.reasoning_effort = medium [model Qwen3.8-27B-xhigh] like = Qwen3.8-27B template.reasoning_effort = xhigh [web] search = searxng url = https://search.example.com/ key = env:EXAMPLE_API_KEY Passive rendering The ImGui paradigm typically uses active rendering , redrawing on vsync
like a video game. This is appropriate in some contexts, like interfaces
within video games. Less so for mostly-static text-oriented UIs, such as a
coding harness. Instead Prospero uses passive rendering with settle
frames to finish animations before going idle. When there’s nothing to
do, Prospero does nothing. It won’t chew on the GPU while the agent is
waiting on a build. Never wait forever An annoyance with most other harnesses is how easily they get stuck. I set
a long-running task, go to sleep, and in the morning find the harness hung
on a trivial issue two hours into the night, wasting the rest. Therefore
Prospero prime design principle: Never wait forever . Every operation
has a deadline. This decision influences everything. If you’re not there
to grant a requested permission, the agent will get a denial by timeout
and must do without. To assist, Prospero will raise a system toast when an
agent requires your attention so that you’re less likely to miss it if
you’re attending. The harness itself plows through intermittent errors , trying its best to
drive the agent to complete its task. All network requests have timeouts,
and watchdogs prevent endless waiting . Agent mailboxes are
bounded . Shell commands that hit their timeout convert to asynchronous background
commands. The agent can continue to wait on them, with a timeout, and so
will be woken at regular intervals to decide if it should continue. The one exception is Plan mode, where it waits indefinitely after offering
a plan or requesting clarification ( ask_user tool). It’s expected that a
user is attending to the agent during Plan mode. No stray processes The harnesses I’ve used have improved, but another regular annoyance
earlier this year was agents starting processes that never get cleaned up.
An agent kicks off a parallel build, hits a timeout because it was too
optimistic, the build “stops” by killing a piece of the build system. But
actually the build continues anyway , at least in part. The agent tries
again, and now two builds are going, interfering with each other, making a
mess and bringing my system to its knees. For awhile I was wary of letting agents run builds in certain harnesses,
which is a terrible outcome. You want agents to close the loop and
iterate independently. A human in the loop is like putting a ball and
chain on the agent, giving up most of its advantages. Prospero promoting a synchronous timeout to an asynchronous task is a huge
improvement on its own, but there’s an additional principle at play: The
whole process tree lives and dies together. When a command is stopped, it
stops . This is trivial on Windows , though few harnesses seem to
take advantage of it. It’s more difficult on macOS and Linux, but Prospero
follows through. Built-in self-help Like every harness, Prospero supports skills , a pre-packaged set of
instructions on how to accomplish some task (“I know kung fu.”). Prospero
contains a skill on itself and can read its built-in documentation.

title: Retired professor arrested for blocking delivery robot. Will do it again
abstract:
Woman vs. machine is playing out in Philadelphia. Matt Rourke/AP Activism See all topics Follow October 14 wasn’t the first time Carolyn Marvin put herself in front of an autonomous delivery robot. It had become, since the wheeled little food vessels were unleashed upon certain parts of Philadelphia, a habit for the 78-year-old: standing in front of one of the robots when she encountered it rolling on the sidewalk, delaying it for a few minutes from delivering its precious lunchtime cargo. But it was the first time that Marvin, a retired University of Pennsylvania communications professor, was arrested for doing it — in a case that she says raises profound questions about public space and the legal protections extended to robots in our increasingly tech-dominated world. “I was under the impression that I had more rights than the robot did,” Marvin said, laughing. Uber Eats launched its self-driving robot delivery fleet in Philly in March, making it the fourth city where meals can be delivered via robot. Not everyone welcomed the heart-eyed little machines: In Philadelphia and elsewhere, videos show people sitting on, vandalizing or kicking the robots. Marvin says the impact of her one-woman protest is limited. “I have a life, so I don’t have tons of time to stand in front of robots,” she said. If she comes across a robot, and it’s “convenient and possible” for her, she might spend 10 or 15 minutes blocking it, moving as it does, to delay it on its journey. The only harm that comes from her hobby is that an office worker’s lunchtime bowl “might be delayed for about 15 minutes at the most,” she said. She views her actions as a symbolic protest against the problems posed by delivery robots: the displacement of low-income delivery workers; the physical hazard the robots pose on the sidewalk; and the privacy concerns posed by the robots’ embedded cameras. “I also think that I have a First Amendment right to protest the abuses of corporations in public space, in the same public space that the robots are occupying,” she said. In the past, she had protested in favor of civil rights, abortion rights, Black Lives Matters, and for ending the Gulf and Vietnam wars. She views her robot mission as an extension of the same impulse: “It’s what we need to do to make sure the government hears the will of the people.” Stopping in front of the robots, Marvin said, led to productive conversations with other passersby who asked what she was doing. Most were supportive, or curious. She never considered that she might be arrested, since, as she said, “I wasn’t impeding any persons. I was impeding a machine.” That’s until the 14th. On the way home from getting her flu shot, Marvin, a jar of enchilada sauce in one hand and chicken biryani takeout in the other, encountered one of the robots and stopped in front of it, per usual. It was in a busy part of the city, and a larger-than-normal crowd began to gather around her. Some were supportive; some were critical. She suspects, she said, that a member of the crowd eventually called the police, who handcuffed her and put her in the back of a squad car, giving her a citation for disorderly conduct. Marvin said one of her friends put it thusly: “Well, you got a disorderly conduct charge for impeding capitalism.” Philadelphia police said that they had responded to a report of “criminal mischief involving a delivery robot.” When they arrived, “officers encountered a female who was refusing to allow a delivery robot to pass,” they wrote in an email. “Police issued multiple commands directing the female to move; however, she refused to comply.” In the aftermath of her arrest, Marvin has found out more about the legal infrastructure that protects robots. In 2020, the Pennsylvania legislature passed a law that classifies autonomous delivery robots — what the law calls “personal delivery devices” — as pedestrians, not vehicles. Democrats, along with labor unions and accessibility advocates, largely opposed the law on the basis that legalizing delivery robots could kill jobs and endanger children and pedestrians; Republicans touted it as an exciting technological advancement. The law means that a vehicle must yield to a delivery robot on crosswalks, just as it would to a person, said John Mattiacci, a Philadelphia personal injury attorney. Still, in theory humans are at the top of the hierarchy: “Personal delivery devices must yield to other pedestrians and pedalcyclists in a pedestrian area,” he said. Uber Eats didn’t respond to a request for comment. Marvin sees the proliferation of delivery robots — and the legal protections of them — as another case of machinery and technology infiltrating everyday life. “There’s a way in which we’ve surrendered the streets to cars long ago, and I don’t think we should surrender the sidewalks to machines,” she said. “Machines in general encroach on our lives,” she went on. “Public space is the most visible place where they’re encroaching on our lives, but they’re going right up the ladder, and lots of people are interested in making that happen.” Most of the technology people encounter day to day is less tangible: the overwhelming adoption of AI, the mysterious social media algorithms that determine the images and narratives the public consumes. The robots, on the other hand, are a clear and visible symbol of the tech takeover, an easy target for anti-tech rage. Her protest, she said, “makes it visible to people and presents the issue in a way that it might not otherwise be presented.” Asked if she plans to get back to blocking robots post-arrest, Marvin was succinct: “Oh yeah.” But now she’ll keep an eye out for the cops. title: Product Managers aren't safe either
abstract:
AI is challenging most jobs, not just devs. And, to me, PM should seriously worrry. Code spitters are cooked, let's be honest here and accept the fate so everyone can move on. Architects aren't, because whatever the accuracy of any model, making it serves you need within the constraints of security + compliance + technical capabilities + budget + ... requires private data, interpersonal meetings and skills that make it hard or impossible to automate today. genAI, to me, feels like the same threat as Instagram for professional photographs: 90% of photographs lost their moat against 16 yo taking pictures with their phones. The remaining 10% unlocked even more value because of their talent, that could not be copied. Now, genAI is threatening devs in the same way: mediocre like me won't survive against 10x developers supercharged with AI (until they also get replaced by supercharged AI agents. But wait? Until they also get replaced by supercharged AI swarms with... bref!) But it's not just devs, mind you! PMs are also severely endangered for the same reasons: when any PM can just prompt a feature, what happens when a dev prompt a feature too? It's up to you to think that PM are better equipped when it comes to understanding why a feature make sense than a developer. What's happening, though, and if you are doing things right, is that the same person coding a feature can also build PM intuition as to why this feature needs to be built at all. The latter comes from LLM. Because since code is cheap, there's more time to invest in understanding the customer pain point and the company solution (not just the soft: the design trade-offs, what were the assumptions 10 years ago versus today, etc...) I grew up with the distinction of "tech guy" needs a "product guy". I am not dismissing it, I am just saying that the world is entering into a phase where both roles are eventually melting into a single function. And that the product guy, whatever his seniority, should be seriously worried*unless he can demonstrate architecture skills, which is one of the last bastion of human intelligence. For the sake of transparency, I am a programmer, I've developed data marketing products for the last four years before moving to Cloudflare to work on their, recently acquired, YC company Zaraz. To close on a more personal note, that doesn't mean I am here to judge: the world is *definitely not* running the way I'd like regarding genAI usage and I am just afraid that "part" and then "our whole" profession disappear. I guess that PMs should be a little more self-aware and start consolidating skills that will work. Like analysing a text file, with a language that lets you do it in just 14 lines of codes

title: Secure Multi-Agent Collaboration Using Large Language Models
abstract:
As Large Language Models have emerged and become increasingly significant, the way to develop smart multi-agent
systems has been transformed, enabling them to communicate, collaborate and decision more efficiently. These systems rely on
agents working independently which need to effectively and safely coordinate their actions, to maintain reliability in messy realworld environments. However, bringing LLMs into the mix introduces new risks like data leaks, trickery from bad actors, and
trust issues. This paper breaks down a full plan for keeping multi-agent teamwork secure when using LLMs. We look at
everything from how they are built and the rules they use to communicate to the safety tools used to stop attacks. We also talk
about where this is being used now, the hurdles we still face, and where the tech is headed for building secure AI ecosystems

title: VAANIX: A Real-Time Voice AI Agent Platform with Action-Enabled Agents, Automated Appointment Booking and a Business Workspace
abstract:
Telephone support is still the main way many small businesses talk to their customers, yet it is also the channel they
are least able to staff around the clock. Traditional IVR menus frustrate callers, and most of the newer AI voice products are
closed, priced per minute and difficult to adapt to a specific business. This paper presents VAANIX, a self-hostable voice agent
platform that connects ordinary phone calls to a streaming pipeline of speech recognition, a large language model and speech
synthesis, so that a caller can simply talk and be understood. The first version of the platform focused on that conversational
pipeline and a developer console. In this paper we describe a second, larger iteration. A single Agent Studio now holds
everything about an agent: its prompt, voice, knowledge base, API settings, call logs, single calls and bulk calling. Agents can
also be given actions at creation time. The most important of these is appointment booking, in which the agent checks
availability while the caller is still on the line, books the slot, and confirms it by voice. Confirmed bookings appear immediately
on a Business Workspace home screen that shows a calendar of the client's own appointments instead of generic call statistics.
We explain the architecture, the action mechanism, the way double bookings are prevented, and the security design built on row
level isolation. Manual testing across all modules showed that callers receive a spoken reply typically within one to two seconds
and that booked slots are reflected on the calendar within moments, without the per-minute platform fees charged by managed
voice agent services.

title: AI-Based College Transportation Management
abstract:
Colleges that run their own buses usually plan transport using fixed routes and estimated student counts. In practice,
the number of students who actually travel changes from day to day, so some buses run with many empty seats while others are
overcrowded. This paper presents the design of the AI-Based College Transportation Decision Support System, a full-stack web
application that collects daily travel confirmations from students and uses rule-based software agents to analyse route-wise
demand, check route compatibility, recommend bus allocation, and suggest seat optimization within capacity limits. Every
recommendation is accompanied by a plain-language explanation, and no change becomes final until the administrator
approves it. The previous allocation stays in force until a replacement plan is approved. The system is built with React.js,
Node.js, Express.js and MongoDB, with JWT-based authentication and role-based access control. It uses predefined rules and
calculations only; it does not use machine learning, GPS tracking, or external generative AI services. This paper describes the
problem, the system architecture, the database design, the rule-based algorithms, and an illustrative worked example.
Experimental evaluation on real college data is identified as future work.

title: Black Swan: Stock Crash Predictor
abstract:
Global financial markets have grown so interconnected and fast-moving that spotting a high-impact event before it
hurts investors' portfolios has become a serious challenge. This project introduces "Black Swan: Stock Crash Predictor," an AIdriven system built to catch unpredictable global events early and gauge how they are likely to ripple through financial markets,
using a combination of Generative AI and Agentic AI. Rather than waiting for a crisis to unfold, the system keeps a constant
watch over news outlets, RSS feeds, financial reports, and live market feeds, flagging emerging risks such as geopolitical
conflict, pandemics, economic downturns, and supply-chain breakdowns as they surface. Generative AI is used to turn this raw
information into readable summaries, forward-looking narratives, and impact assessments, so investors can make sense of
complicated situations quickly. Agentic AI adds a further layer of autonomy, allowing the system to reason independently, make
decisions on its own, and keep adjusting to shifting market conditions. It also runs automated stress-testing simulations and risk
assessments to gauge how markets and investments might behave under uncertainty. Where conventional monitoring tools tend
to fall behind fast-changing events, this approach is built to keep pace, offering proactive alerts that give investors an early
warning. Overall, the framework is aimed at sharpening key decision-making factors: response time, prediction accuracy, market
awareness, and investment strategy planning.

title: A TIERED LIFECYCLE GOVERNANCE FRAMEWORK FOR AGENTIC ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN FINANCIAL SERVICES
abstract: The rapid emergence of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) presents significant governance challenges for financial services, where autonomous systems increasingly support high-impact financial activities. Existing regulatory approaches remain fragmented and continue to rely primarily on non-binding supervisory guidance, leaving important gaps in lifecycle oversight, accountability, and systemic risk management. This paper proposes the Tiered Lifecycle Governance (TLG) Framework, a strategic governance model that integrates lifecycle-based AI oversight with responsive, risk-based regulation. The framework combines three transaction-risk tiers with four AI lifecycle stages to establish proportionate oversight obligations that balance innovation, regulatory accountability, and financial stability. Drawing on technological, economic, legal, and institutional perspectives, the framework is applied to the 2026 U.S. interagency review of model risk management guidance (SR 26-2) to demonstrate how lifecycle governance can strengthen oversight of agentic AI in financial services. The analysis shows that the TLG Framework provides a structured alternative to the existing guidance-versus-rulemaking approach by aligning regulatory obligations with transaction risk rather than institutional size or technology labels. The paper concludes that binding, lifecycle-based oversight offers a practical pathway for improving resilience, transparency, and accountability in financial AI governance while providing a transferable governance model for other emerging AI policy domains.

title: AI-Assisted Web Server Log Interpretation Using LLaMA Model
abstract:
Modern web infrastructures generate large volumes of access logs that contain valuable information related to system
activity, user behaviour, performance monitoring, and cybersecurity threats. Manual analysis of these logs is time-consuming,
error-prone, and inefficient for detecting suspicious activities in real time. This project presents the design and implementation
of a Local AI System for Log Interpretation using LLaMA models, capable of performing automated log analysis, anomaly
detection, AI-assisted summarization, and conversational log investigation within a privacy-preserving local execution
environment. The system integrates Django-based operational management, Linux scheduling utilities (Cron and At), quantized
GGUF(GPT-Generated Unified Format) LLaMA models, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) techniques to support
both scheduled analysis workflows and interactive “Chat with AI” operations. The log files uploaded/access from read-only
specified location are passed to the AI inference engine, where log parsing, OWASP-based threat detection, contextual analysis,
and structured JSON response generation are performed using locally deployed LLaMA models.
Through CPU-compatible inference utilising llama-cpp-python, the project maintains lightweight deployment while enabling
instantaneous, recurring, and scheduled analysis execution. GPU-accelerated environments such as Google Colab and Kaggle
were additionally utilized for large-scale inference evaluation and high-volume log processing experiments. The conversational
RAG workflow enables users to interact directly with uploaded logs using natural language queries and receive AI-generated
cybersecurity insights, suspicious activity explanations, and remediation recommendations.
Experimental evaluation demonstrates reliable task execution, efficient response generation, structured report handling, and
effective contextual reasoning capabilities for both scheduled analysis and conversational AI-assisted workflows. The proposed
system provides a modular, privacy-preserving, and locally deployable solution for intelligent cybersecurity log analysis and
operational threat interpretation.

title: CONSTRUCTING PROFESSIONAL IDENTITIES IN AI-ENHANCED LANGUAGE CLASSROOM: A STUDY OF PAKISTANI ENGLISH LANGUAGE TEACHERS’ PERSPECTIVES AND PRACTICES
abstract: The main aim of the study is to investigate the construction of English Language Teachers’ (ELTs) professional identity in the Artificial Intelligence (AI) era in the Pakistani Punjab context. The qualitative analysis is embedded in semi-structured interviews. Multilayered sampling techniques were used, and data were collected from ELTs working in public and private educational institutions and analyzed using the Grounded Theory Approach (GTA). Initially, purposive sampling was used to identify appropriate samples, and those samples referred additional samples until saturation was attained on the thirteenth sample. The investigation was theoretically informed by Gee’s (2000) distinction between I-identity and A-identity. Findings created five interrelated categories: Institutionally Framed Professionalism, Agentive Professional Self, Constrained Autonomy, Negotiation Professional Identity, and Hybrid Identity Construction. Results highlight that examination-driven systems, curricular mandates, and administrative checks and balances powerfully form ELTs’ identities. They are sustained simultaneously by contemplative practice, adaptive strategies, and professional achievement. Autonomy was developed as conditional rather than absolute, leading teachers to negotiate between organizational compliance and personal pedagogical obligation. The study demonstrates that ELT identity in Punjab is dynamic, context-sensitive, and permanently negotiated. By integrating hierarchical and agentive dimensions of identity, this research contributes to a nuanced understanding of teacher professionalism within examination- focused educational systems.

title: LAYER 2 OF THE AI-FIRST SDLC: A PROPOSED AGENT-DRIVEN ARCHITECTURE FOR BUILD, VALIDATION, AND RELEASE READINESS
abstract: This paper proposes Layer 2 of the AI-First Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC) introduced in our parent framework and extended through the Layer 1 Product and Designer Layer. Layer 2 is a conceptual Build, Validate, and Release architecture intended to transform a Product Requirement Bundle (PRB) and a Design Artifact Bundle (DAB) into a documented, validated, merge-ready pull request. It defines six proposed specialist agents—Architecture, Coding, Testing, Review, PR, and CI Gate—coordinated by a Layer 2 Sub-Orchestrator. The design includes a bounded Feedback-Driven Repair Loop, revalidation after code modifications, non-overridable CI and security gates, and a mandatory human merge decision. The proposed design draws on the authors' technical analysis, review of existing software-engineering and agentic-AI approaches, and exploratory proof-of-concept work. The integrated architecture has not been implemented or empirically evaluated; potential effects on delivery time, code quality, cost, and compliance remain hypotheses for future evaluation.

title: AI Fitness OS: Verifiable, Multi-Metric Fitness Guidance by Constraining a Large Language Model with Deterministically Computed Targets
abstract:
Fitness applications usually record one behaviour in isolation, and large-language-model (LLM) coaches produce
fluent advice whose numbers are rarely checked. This paper presents AI Fitness OS, a web application that keeps training,
nutrition, hydration, sleep, weight, steps and goals in one per-user record, computes every numerical target deterministically
from published equations and stated heuristics, and passes those targets to Google Gemini as binding constraints; each
generated meal plan is re-checked in code against a ±5 % tolerance. The premise was examined through secondary research on
a public dataset of 2,111 records, and the artefact through tests, simulation and live measurement. All eight lifestyle metrics that
the system tracks or addresses were significantly associated with obesity level (Bonferroni-adjusted α = 0.00625), although only
three remained so on 515 records resembling the original survey. A Random Forest that combined the eight metrics reached a
macro-F1 of 0.720 against 0.263 for the best single metric (Wilcoxon W = 55, p = 0.00098). Across 1,000 simulated user profiles,
every constrained meal plan fell within ±5 % of its calorie target, against 75 of 1,000 unconstrained plans (exact McNemar p <
10⁻²⁰⁰). The calculator agreed with the dataset's weight-category labels for 98.82 % of records, and live responses took 2.5–6.1 s
at no cost. The findings support computing arithmetic, generating language and checking the output against the computed
numbers.

title: FROM AIOPS TO AGENTOPS: SERVICE-LEVEL OBJECTIVES AND ERROR-BUDGET-GOVERNED AUTONOMY FOR PRODUCTION AI AGENTS
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now run production workflows, including IT and network operations, yet they are usually monitored with signals designed for deterministic services: availability, latency, and error rate. An agent can satisfy all three while completing the wrong task. This paper extends AIOps-style service management to agentic systems. It contributes a layered set of service-level indicators (SLIs) covering platform health, step-level tool use, verified task outcomes, and guardrail integrity; a taxonomy of seven agent failure classes mapped to the signals that expose them; and an error-budget policy that governs an agent's autonomy as well as its release cadence. A Monte Carlo simulation of a production operations agent evaluates the approach across 2,100 injected incidents. Conventional platform monitoring detected only platform failures, firing in at most 1.7% of runs for the other six classes. Burn-rate alerting on verified task outcomes detected every class in 89.7% to 100% of runs within 24 hours, with no false alarms, but took a median of 3.5 to 10.6 hours under standard thresholds. A change-aware rule, active for six hours after a deployment or model change, cut median detection of change-induced regressions to 44 to 63 minutes at a cost of about one additional page per month. The results support layered, outcome-based service-level objectives as the operational basis for production agents.

title: EVALUATING PATH EFFICIENCY AND WHEEL DYNAMICS ACROSS VARYING TURNING RADII IN WHEELED MOBILE ROBOTS
abstract: Mobile robots navigating within indoor confined spaces generally use various turning techniques to negotiate obstacles and corners. Although zero radius turns (R=0.0 m) allow saving space, the continuous-arc approach provides different possibilities related to such factors as energy, duration, and wheel slip. This paper proposes an analysis of the performances of a mobile robot based on a simulation carried out using the Python programming language and NumPy package. The study examines a model of a differential-drive robot making a 90-degree turn at different radii (R ∈ {0.0,0.2,0.5,1.0,2.0}m). On the basis of the kinematic analysis along with power and slip estimations, it has been demonstrated that small radii (for example, R=0.2 m) reduce greatly the duration of the manoeuvre (0.78 s) and save space, although they increase significantly the power peaks (6.30 W) and slip peaks (0.0141). In its turn, large radii (R=2.0 m) decrease mechanical slips and power peaks but increase energy consumption (37.92 J) and manoeuvre duration (7.85 s). Composite Efficiency Index indicates that larger arcs lead to increased efficiency per joule, while small turns increase speed efficiency. These simulation findings give us a mathematical basis for determining adaptive turns depending on operating conditions, such as choosing between battery life and time efficiency.

title: ATLAS - Where Travel Meets AI: An AI-Powered Travel Planning and Decision-Support Platform with Live Data Grounding
abstract:
Travel planning is a fragmented, multi-domain decision process: a traveller must separately research destinations,
transport, accommodation, food, activities and weather before assembling a feasible schedule. This paper presents ATLAS
(“Where Travel Meets AI”), an implemented AI-powered travel planning and decision-support platform that pairs a large language model (LLM) planner with deterministic grounding against live geospatial and environmental data. Given a destination,
an inclusive date range, a boarding location, a budget and traveller preferences, ATLAS generates a day-by-day itinerary with
the open-weight gpt-oss-120b model served through Groq, while route, weather, food and accommodation agents run concurrently and record the provenance of each data source. Model output is validated rather than trusted: a schema enforces exactly
one itinerary day per requested calendar date, generated place names are resolved through OpenStreetMap’s Nominatim geocoder, and road distances and travel times are computed with OSRM from the traveller’s real boarding location, with unknown
legs reported as unavailable instead of zero. The system is implemented as a React and TypeScript single-page application
backed by FastAPI and PostgreSQL, and includes a live weather outlook, real restaurant and attraction listings, a simulated
booking flow that issues a PDF e-ticket by e-mail, and a community Lost & Found module. We describe the architecture and
grounding method, report a verification suite of 477 automated tests and preliminary functional observations, and state the system’s current limitations explicitly

title: HOW RELIABLE ARE LAYER COMPARISONS FROM SMALL PROBING DATASETS
abstract: Probing classifiers are used to compare the linguistic information available at different layers of a language model. These comparisons often rely on limited labelled data, although additional training examples can change which layer performs best. We study the accuracy lost when a layer is selected from a small probing dataset and then evaluated with a probe trained on more data. Experiments across encoder and decoder models show that changes in the selected layer are frequent, but many produce little loss in accuracy. Larger losses depend on the checkpoint and, within the examined Qwen3 family, concentrate in the smaller models. In most such cases, the initially selected layer has higher test accuracy with limited data, but another layer benefits more from additional training. Simple geometric scores often make less accurate choices than a fitted linear probe. Controlled experiments also show how feature scaling affects the regularized probe without removing information. Finally, uncertainty estimates for fixed probes do not consistently predict selection errors after further training. The findings support evaluating the accuracy cost of layer selection directly and distinguishing uncertainty about current predictions from changes caused by additional training data.

title: A Study on the Process of Constructing Generative AI Image Prompts Using Hairstyle Search Interest: Focusing on Google Trends Analysis and the Procedural Application of the PDCA Framework
abstract: This study aimed to analyze online search interest in hairstyle-related terms and to explore a procedure for converting the results into a data-based structured prompt for generative AI hairstyle image creation. The PDCA (Plan-Do-Check-Act) framework was used as a procedural framework. Google Trends data for seven hairstyle-related terms were analyzed from April 2021 to March 2026, and Sleek Cut, which showed the highest Recent Interest Ratio (2.03), was selected as the case hairstyle. Based on hair design elements and prompt engineering studies, the prompt was structured into Basic, Detailed, and Control elements using R and applied to Google Gemini 20 times to generate 20 images. Three hair and beauty experts independently evaluated the images using five criteria. The overall mean was 4.50, with form showing the highest score (M=4.63) and color the lowest (M=4.15). Average-measure ICCs ranged from .887 to .968, with an overall ICC of .948, indicating high inter-rater agreement. Based on these results, color-related prompt elements were identified as requiring further refinement. The Act stage was limited to deriving improvement directions and did not include regeneration or re-evaluation. These findings suggest that online search-interest data can be used as an exploratory basis for selecting hairstyle visualization targets and systematically structuring prompt elements for generative AI.

title: SECURING THE AI-FIRST SDLC: IDENTITY, ACCESS, AND DATA PROTECTION FOR ENTERPRISE AI AGENTS
abstract: AI agents can now participate in several steps of software delivery: reading requirements, changing code, requesting tests, and preparing releases. Giving them this freedom creates a difficult security question. How can an enterprise allow useful work without giving an agent more authority than the task requires? Existing practices such as least privilege, identity management, separation of duties, and audit logging provide much of the foundation. The challenge is applying them consistently when a human delegates work to agents that use several connected systems. This paper proposes Agentic Identity and Access Governance (AIAG), a security framework for the AI-First Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC). Four connected mechanisms define the proposal: a Role Conflict Matrix that checks the combined permissions of people and their sponsored agents; an Agent Access Manifest that records permitted tools and operating limits; a governed boundary between live personal-information access and general AI-assisted work; and an MCP Gateway that enforces access policy before tool calls execute. A customer notification-preference change is used to explain how these mechanisms affect development, testing, release approval, and support. We also describe credential handling, data-egress controls, audit, and practical ways to evaluate the framework. The work is conceptual, informed by technical analysis and exploratory proof-of-concept activity. No end-to-end deployment or measured security results are claimed.
